Yeah, if you limit the thought experiment to relativistic concepts, then you're talking about generational arks like the article puts forward. And frankly, I can't see humanity coming together for something like that over anything short of its own pending demise, considering the resources that would go into just one such ship, never mind the fleet that would be required to ensure successful colonization.

Crack the book on scifi, which, let's be honest, that's all this really is, and pull out FTL, and that's no longer the case. Trips that might otherwise take hundreds or thousands of years could be accomplished in a decade or less -- instantaneously for some ideas that aren't even based on fiction, such as wormholes. There's a lot of fictional wiggle room for a fictional idea if you skirt around the doom-and-gloom of trying to introduce reality into it.

Kim Stanley Robinson, the author of the article, is a science fiction writer, and one of the better ones, in my estimation. Check out the Mars Trilogy if you have not done so already. I think it's safe to say he'd really like it if there were plausible ways to overcome these limits. I plan to posit a workaround (not a fix, but a workaround) in my own work, which will basically involve time dilation for the inhabitants of the ship. It may still take tens of thousands of years to get where they're going, but it will only seem like a couple weeks to them. That means only needing a couple weeks worth of food and water, and not having to worry a whole lot about sustainability, entertainment, or dealing with babies. The main problem they're going to encounter is that most of the good real estate in their destination system is already inhabited by people who left later but had better engines, and thus got there hundreds or thousands of years before.

I'm not trying to disrespect anyone's position as a writer or a theorist. Indeed, the article drops the "science fiction" bomb in the second sentence, and that didn't go unnoticed. I'm just responding to the initial question asked by the submitter, and then the followup.

Replace by fee

One problem with using fees to control congestion is that the fee to get to the front of the queue might change after you made a payment. Bitcoin Core has a brilliant solution to this problem — allow people to mark their payments as changeable after they’ve been sent, up until they appear in the block chain. The stated intention is to let people adjust the fee paid, but in fact their change also allows people to change the payment to point back to themselves, thus reversing it.

At a stroke, this makes using Bitcoin useless for actually buying things, as you’d have to wait for a buyer’s transaction to appear in the block chain … which from now on can take hours rather than minutes, due to the congestion.

Core’s reasoning for why this is OK goes like this: it’s no big loss because if you hadn’t been waiting for a block before, there was a theoretical risk of payment fraud, which means you weren’t using Bitcoin properly. Thus, making that risk a 100% certainty doesn’t really change anything.

In other words, they don’t recognise that risk management exists and so perceive this change as zero cost.

This protocol change will be released with the next version of Core (0.12), so will activate when the miners upgrade. It was massively condemned by the entire Bitcoin community but the remaining Bitcoin Core developers don’t care what other people think, so the change will happen.

If that didn’t convince you Bitcoin has serious problems, nothing will. How many people would think bitcoins are worth hundreds of dollars each when you soon won’t be able to use them in actual shops?
